findings.title: Haste places harm inside the name of good
findings.claim: The focus keeps the ordinary act of calling for an object and sets harm against good under a final diagnosis of haste: the caller's wish can rush ahead of judging what the object does. In the pericope, this rushing can also carry a bounded image of provision sought before its time, while the request remains distinct from the distribution that follows.
findings.mechanism: The call draws a desired object toward its speaker; the focus places harm and good in parallel, then names the human hasty. The nearby contrast between the immediate and later striving, followed by differentiated gifts, makes the hurry resemble a demand for early receipt before value is weighed. This changes the call from a mere utterance into a valuation error under temporal pressure, without making the petition an allocation command.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see how one desire mechanism may be aimed at harm while being experienced as a request for good, and how haste compresses wanting, judging, and receiving.
findings.containment: The ordinary call and good-versus-harm contrast remain intact. The quick-provision branch is analogical: its boundary restricts it to food or provision and does not make the focus adjective for haste mean food. The branch for God bringing an unwanted hardship is excluded because its own boundary says it is not a verbal wish for evil, while the focus has a human caller. The later distribution does not show that a call commands its outcome.

epistemic.reason: The focus words directly ground calling, good, harm, and haste. The provision image is retained only as a bounded analogy supported by the pericope's immediate/later and allocation context.

findings.reader_payoff: Haste acquires an epistemic dimension: desire arrives before inspection and distinction have finished their work.

findings.title: The harmful call inside a returning cycle
findings.claim: The focus's call can be heard within a recursive pericope sequence: repeated rupture, returned advantage, and good or harm directed back to the actors make a one-way utterance capable of entering a cycle that returns to the same human.
findings.mechanism: The focus supplies a call for harm and a branch image of successive collapse. In 17:4-8 the context marks events as occurring twice, returns an advantage, pairs good and harm with the self, and closes with a repeated return formula. Contact with those returns changes the call from a single outward act into a possible participant in a reflexive sequence.
findings.reader_payoff: The consequence of a hasty call can be seen as a loop through the caller and the caller's community, not only as an effect that travels away once.
findings.containment: The 17:4-8 sequence is also a collective historical cycle. Its verses do not state that this particular human call causes that history, and the connection records describe the relation to invocation as broad or indirect. The collapse branch is a contextual image of propagation, not a literal gloss of the focus verb.

epistemic.reason: The exact roots and coordinates of all eight trace branches match the packet. The recursive reading survives as attributed context while the collective-historical alternative remains live.

findings.title: Good tested by a guided course
findings.claim: The focus's requested good can be heard as the better outcome to be chosen, while the preceding context gives a standard beyond immediate attraction: guidance toward what is upright, fitting action, and a resulting reward. findings.reader_payoff: A wish's intensity no longer supplies its own measure; a nearby standard of direction and action comes into view.
findings.containment: Verse 17:9 does not define the focus term khayr or prove that every request refers to its path. It supplies a contextual criterion that the human may fail to use. The alternative reading of 17:9 as a promise without a lexical definition remains live.

epistemic.reason: All seven trace coordinates match. The connection row identifies guidance before the hasty human; identifying that as the focus's criterion remains an inference.

findings.title: Haste as a choice of horizon
findings.claim: Haste can name a value horizon, not only fast speech: the human treats what arrives immediately as good even when its terminal path is harmful, while the later good is joined to sustained striving. The call is set beside a distinction between immediate receipt and a longer course.
findings.mechanism: The focus's haste branch meets 17:18, where the immediate is desired and acceleration is selective, and 17:19, where the later horizon is sought through effort. The preceding 17:10 adds a rejected afterlife and painful consequence. These contacts change haste from an impulse within one request into a way of valuing by arrival time.
findings.reader_payoff: A hidden criterion inside haste becomes visible: what comes quickly can be rated as good before its later consequence is considered.
findings.containment: The focus may still describe rash speech more narrowly, while 17:18-19 classify different life aims. This finding keeps both readings available and does not equate every call with rejection of the later horizon.

epistemic.reason: All eight unique branch refs and their context coordinates match. The immediate/later contrast is explicit, while its role as the focus's valuation rule remains attributed.
